sentences.text: Task 4, Fatima is telling Charlie about an interview she had with Albert Wan, a retired toy factory worker in Hong Kong.
Listen to their conversation and complete the answers below, Please note that you do not need to answer in complete sentences.
You now have 30 seconds to study the task.
At the end of the task, you will have three minutes to tidy up your answers.
So how was your interview with Albert Wann then?
It was great to be honest.
He was telling me that he worked in the same toy factory, Macro Toys, in Kuntong, for almost 30 years.
He was born in a tiny village in China and because his family didn’t have much, he decided to go to Shanghai.
Like a lot of people did in search of a better life.
Yeah, it’s a very common story in China at that time.
And it was there he got 3 months of training to earned to make toys in a factory.
And presumably he then came to Hong Kong because of the war or something.
No no, it was after that.
He said that he came with all of his friends from the factory in Shanghai.
The representatives of Makro Toys came from Hong Kong to Shanghai high, and they recruited about a hundred of them in Shanghai, paid for their shipfare, and took them to Hong Kong.
Wow, can you imagine?
All of your friends together off the Hong Kong.
Must have been a big adventure.
Yeah. And did Albert give a sense of how he fell towards his employers, the factory owners,
the additional benefits workers received, He did say that initially at least they were paid a really small amount but he explained that the additional benefits really helped them save a lot
of the money they did make.
So, the additional benefits were really important.
So, what do you mean by additional benefits?
Do you mean like fringe benefits, like health insurance and bonuses, that sort of thing?
well, sort of.
The first additional benefit he mentioned was that the factory provided dormitories for them to stay in.
This is more or less unheard of in Hong Kong nowadays but factory dormitories were common back then.
And interestingly enough he spoke about the importance of the canteen.
So, all the workers got free food.
So that was an additional benefit and really important.
And you said that this changed.
Yes, well, for Albert at least.
He was promoted to being a manager eventually and so he ended up with quite a comfortable salary.
And did the benefits change?
Well, he said that as the workforce became more established in Hong Kong, people started having families so the factory actually built flats for the families to live in for free.
That’s interesting. You do still see old blocks of flats built by factories in Hong Kong.
The good and the bad things.
I see. I mean, we hear of some horror stories about factory working conditions in Hong Kong.
Yeah, and this was pretty interesting.
He spoke about working for 12 hours in a row standing up.
So that was pretty tough.
Indeed. Indeed, that does sound tough.
Especially standing. But he did say that they had great conversations with the people as they worked for twelve hours together.
There was a great atmosphere among them.
He loved the banter, the conversations, the jokes between them.
He did emphasise that.
And what else?
He spoke about the great pride in the toys they were making and how he was proud to be making toys that made children happy.
Interesting. You forget that factory workers have that sense of pride in what they’re doing.
So yeah. That was interesting to hear.
Oh, and I almost forgot.
He said in the summer the heat was unbearable because there were no windows and no air con in the factory of course.
So, it was incredibly hot where they were working.
Sounds awful. And did you ask him about accidents in the factory?
There must have been loads.
Yes, Albert said that he didn’t remember any.
Hmm. Yeah, that’s what I was thinking.
Either Neither Albert is telling the truth and there were no accidents that the factory and Macro Toys had the best safety record in Hong Kong.
Yeah right. Or the world Or his memory is failing and he can’t remember because it’s so long ago.
He is in his 80s, But I don’t think that’s it because his memory was perfectly fine with everything else.
Maybe he wants to be loyal to the factory and the owners and just not tell us.
Exactly. I think you’re right.
He didn’t want to tell you because he was being loyal to the factory and the owners.
Yeah. And speaking of which he spoke about when the factory closed down and how he felt about it.
Oh, really? Yes, he was a manager by the time that the factory closed down.
Quite successful you might say.
So, when the factory closed everybody in the factory, all the workers, lost their job but he was kept on, but not as a manager but as a security guard, guarding the empty factory building.
Hmm and That’s quite a picture.
Going from being a manager with all the noise and activity and his friends and colleagues to being alone guarding an old empty factory.
Yeah, I know.
But he still stays in touch with the other factory workers he worked with.
Does he? That’s good.
Yeah, a really interesting old guy Albert.
